title: Your brain can hear a bass note that isn’t actually there
body: A musical note usually contains a fundamental frequency plus overtones at whole-number multiples of it. Remove the fundamental but keep the overtones, and listeners still hear the same pitch, because the brain infers it from the spacing of the harmonics. That is why a deep voice still sounds deep over a traditional phone line, which cuts off frequencies below about 300 Hz, and why tiny speakers can suggest bass they cannot produce.

slides.question: A traditional phone line throws away everything below a certain frequency. Where is the cut-off?
slides.explanation: About 300 Hz. A traditional line carries roughly 300–3,400 Hz, so a deep voice’s fundamental never arrives; your brain rebuilds the pitch from the spacing of the harmonics that do.

slides.question: A note’s lowest frequency is its fundamental. How does the brain work out a pitch whose fundamental is missing?
options: From the spacing of the harmonics
slides.explanation: Overtones sit at whole-number multiples of the fundamental, so their spacing gives it away. That is why a deep voice still sounds deep over a phone line.

slides.heading: Which is not a harmonic of a 100 Hz note?
slides.explanation: Harmonics sit at whole-number multiples of the fundamental: 200, 300, 400 and 500 Hz. 450 Hz is 4.5 times 100, so it doesn’t belong.
